title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: How Stuntmen (and -women) Work
summary: Summer Movie Playlist rerun of the 2013 Stuff You Should Know episode on how stuntmen and stuntwomen work. The hosts cover the history of movie stunts from slapstick comedians like Buster Keaton through westerns, the 1960s-70s technology boom (squibs, air rams, airbags), and the shift toward CGI. They discuss why productions hire stunt performers (safety, cost, and specialized skills), the role of the stunt coordinator and second unit director, and techniques such as poor man's process, stage fighting, squibs and pre-drilled bullet holes, fire stunts, and falls. They also cover notable incidents (Vic Morrow on Twilight Zone, Brandon Lee on The Crow, Hell's Angels deaths), how to break into the field (start as a PA or extra, get to know stunt coordinators, specialize, stunt schools), and actors who perform their own stunts. The episode ends with listener mail about verbal tics and sign-off plugs.

segments.title: Opening banter and The Fall Guy
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the rerun and joke about The Fall Guy theme and its stuntman premise. They note stunt performers rarely get recognition and that the Academy has no stunt category, though stunt awards exist.

segments.title: Definition and early history of stunts
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish movie stunt people from other stunt performers and explain that stunts exist to make violence look real. They describe early stunts in slapstick comedy, including Buster Keaton's Steamboat Bill, Jr. house-facade stunt, and note that early stunt performers were often cross-dressed men playing women.

segments.title: Growth of the stunt field
segments.summary: As westerns and action films grew in the early twentieth century, horse riders and other specialists became stunt performers, and dedicated doubles for stars developed.

segments.title: Stunt technology and modern safety
segments.summary: The hosts describe 1960s and 1970s developments such as squibs and air rams, plus airbags and car cages, and note the shift toward CGI, with an example criticized in Kingdom of the Crystal Skull. They say safety has improved while risk remains.

segments.title: Why productions hire stunt people
segments.summary: The hosts explain that stunt performers are hired for safety, for specialized skills, and for cost and scheduling, including second-unit shooting. Movies typically mix CGI, stunt performers, and actors doing their own fighting.

segments.title: Process trailers and car stunts
segments.summary: The hosts describe car filming methods: camera rigs on real cars, cars on process trailers pulled by trucks, and poor man's process where a stationary car is pushed and lit to look like it is moving.

segments.title: Actors who do their own stunts
segments.summary: Tom Cruise is named as an actor who does his own stunts, and the hosts reflect on whether they would do stunts themselves.

segments.title: Deaths and injuries on set
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the history of on-set deaths, including Hell's Angels under Howard Hughes and the Twilight Zone: The Movie helicopter accident that killed Vic Morrow and two children. They also describe the assistant director's responsibility for safety, including gun checks.

segments.title: Pay, work scarcity, and the job's demands
segments.summary: The hosts say stunt pay can be good for experienced performers but work is scarce and competitive. They describe long rehearsal hours, measurements, pyrotechnics, and standing in water for long days, and note the goal of anonymity.

segments.title: Stunt coordinator and second unit roles
segments.summary: The stunt coordinator hires stunt performers, plans and oversees stunts, and runs the stunt department with its own budget. The second unit director often is a former stunt performer or coordinator.

segments.title: Stage fighting, punches, and squibs
segments.summary: The hosts explain stage fighting and selling punches with camera angles and sound effects, plus ramps for fly-through punches. They describe squibs as chest-plate blood packets triggered electronically and the pre-drilled, patched bullet holes in walls. They mention multi-camera setups for dangerous shots.

segments.title: Blanks, Quentin Tarantino squibs, and Brandon Lee
segments.summary: The hosts describe blank cartridges containing gunpowder and wadding, and mention Brandon Lee's death on The Crow from a bullet lodged in a barrel. They also mention Tarantino's use of real squibs in Django Unchained.

segments.title: Falls, airbags, and Dar Robinson
segments.summary: The hosts discuss falls onto airbags and cardboard boxes, and mention Dar Robinson's famous fall through a window of the Peachtree Plaza Hotel in Sharky's Machine. They note stunt performers are sensible professionals focused on safety.

segments.title: Fire stunts and explosions
segments.summary: The hosts describe fire stunts with fire-retardant clothing, flammable gel, hoods with oxygen, and timed extinguishing. They also discuss force perspective and air ram explosions, citing Commando.

segments.title: Car stunts, rams, and Hooper
segments.summary: Car flips are done with rams or ramps, and the hosts discuss Hal Needham's Hooper, a film about an aging stuntman starring Burt Reynolds.

segments.title: How to become a stunt performer
segments.summary: The hosts describe an apprenticeship-style path: start as an extra or PA, join the Screen Actors Guild, get to know stunt coordinators, and submit a headshot. Stunt schools like Rick Seaman Stunt Driving School and International Stunt School exist, but there is no degree path. Specializing in one skill helps get in.

segments.title: Books and stunt performers' skills
segments.summary: The hosts list books on stunts and discuss stunt performers' backgrounds in motorcycle racing, car driving, and skiing, including a Bond ski chase.

segments.title: Celebrity stunts and famous stunt scenes
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Zoe Bell's hood-hanging stunt in Death Proof, Burt Reynolds and Burt Lancaster doing their own stunts, Joe Canutt's Ben-Hur chariot save, and Tom Cruise's Mission: Impossible climb in Moab. They name women and actors known for stunts, including Gina Carano in Haywire.

segments.title: Promo for TV show and related episode notes
segments.summary: The hosts mention the TV show airing on Science Channel and the HowStuffWorks search bar. Brief promotional segment.

segments.title: Listener mail on verbal tics
segments.summary: A listener points out the hosts say 'like' and other phrases often; the hosts respond and joke about their habits, and the listener's list of frequent phrases is read.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact information
segments.summary: The hosts remind listeners of the TV premiere and iTunes availability, then give social media and email contact details and sign off.
